cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in tate-chu-yoko composition. — JA: どの文字も縦中横の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: § A.30 is one sentence in each locale and nothing else: no table, no key, no Remarks cell. The sentence is a universal admission and not an empty enumeration, and the difference between those two readings is the whole of this file. Read as a property of the code point it makes every occurrence in the document a member of cl-30 and the other twenty-nine classes unreachable, which is absurd; read as JLReq states it — 「どの文字も縦中横の文字として使うことができる」, any character may be used as a character of tate-chu-yoko (縦中横) — it says that nothing about a character disqualifies it and that something else decides. What decides is the construct, which is what § 3.9.2's own name for the class says: 縦中横中の文字, the characters *within* a tate-chu-yoko. The occurrence asked about is the first digit of the two-digit number § 2.3.2 names as the usual application of the construct. It declares the half em frame (字幅) because § 3.2.3 states that frame for the interior — 'Proportional glyphs (or half-width glyphs for European numerals) are used for characters in tate-chu-yoko layout' — and the case is set in vertical composition because the construct exists only there: the glossary defines tate-chu-yoko as 「縦組の行中で，文字を縦向きのまま横組にすること」 and § 2.3.2 lists it as the third of three ways of setting Latin letters and European numerals in vertical writing mode. That is a direction condition on the construct's availability and not on § A.30's sentence, which carries no direction qualifier at all; spec/derived/rules.tsv accordingly marks § 3.2.5, the handling rule, direction_conditional and marks no membership statement.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ A.30, § 3.9.2's entry for cl-30, § 3.2.3's third style)

forbidden.why: Reading the key and the frame and never asking which construct the occurrence is in. § A.24 lists U+0032 with the Remark 'half-width' (字幅は半角) and § 3.2.6's Note states that 'half- and fixed-width European numerals, when mixed with Japanese text, are treated as members of the grouped numerals (cl-24) class', so this is the answer a total function from a folded key and a frame to a class must give. Under such an implementation cl-30 is unreachable for every input, because § A.30 enumerates no key that could reach it.

cases.quote: EN: Any character may participate in tate-chu-yoko composition. — JA: どの文字も縦中横の文字として使うことができる．
cases.rationale: The same run, asked about its second occurrence. § A.30's sentence is a permission over characters and it is unqualified, so nothing distinguishes the second digit from the first; § 3.2.5 sets the interior 'from left to right using solid setting', which is a statement about the spaces *between* the characters of the run and therefore about a run with more than one of them. C.2#13 and E.2#12 both speak of characters 「縦中横中の文字（cl-30）の文字」 belonging to a tate-chu-yoko group, which requires every character of the group to be a member and not only its head. This occurrence is the one an implementation that maps a construct to its first item silently drops, and the drop is invisible in the class of the run as a whole: it shows up as a break opportunity inside a two-digit number, which C.2#13 forbids.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ A.30, § 3.9.2's entry for cl-30, § 3.2.5's interior setting)

forbidden.why: Classifying the head of the construct and reading the key for the rest. The two digits are one tate-chu-yoko group: C.2#13 denies a break between two consecutive characters of one group, and a second digit answered cl-24 would take the ordinary grouped-numeral treatment inside a construct § 3.2.5 sets solid.

cases.quote: EN: Proportional glyphs (or half-width glyphs for European numerals) are used for characters in tate-chu-yoko layout. — JA: この場合，プロポーショナルな文字（又はアラビア数字は半角の文字）を用いる．
cases.rationale: The differential twin of A.30/two-digit-number/first-digit, and the reason that case is worth publishing. The same code point in the same construct is declared on the proportional frame instead of the half em one — the other of the two the quoted sentence names — and the key's answer changes underneath while the expectation below does not: § A.27 lists U+0032 with the Remark 'proportionally-spaced' (プロポーショナル) and § 3.2.6's Note treats proportional European numerals as cl-27, so an implementation reading the key answers cl-24 in the case above and cl-27 here. The expected answer is byte-identical to the one there, and that identity is the assertion. § A.30 has no Remarks column to draw a frame distinction in, so the axis that disambiguates 42 percent of Appendix A's enumerated keys is inert for this class; the quoted sentence of § 3.2.3 is an instruction about how the run is set, not a condition on membership, and a caller who declares the other frame has set the run the other way the same sentence permits.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ A.30, § 3.9.2's entry for cl-30, § 3.2.3's frame instruction)

forbidden.why: The key's answer on this frame. § A.27's Remark and § 3.2.6's Note both name a proportional European numeral as cl-27, and an implementation that answers it here answers cl-24 for the identical occurrence one case earlier — two different classes for one construct, decided by a glyph the caller happened to choose.

cases.quote: EN: The character advance of commas (cl-07), full stops (cl-06), opening brackets (cl-01), closing brackets (cl-02) and middle dots (cl-05) is half-width (half em). — JA: 読点類（cl-07），句点類（cl-06），始め括弧類（cl-01），終わり括弧類（cl-02）及び中点類（cl-05）の文字の大きさは，二分（二分アキ）である．
cases.rationale: § 3.1.2 names the five classes whose occurrences must declare a frame, and the requirement is keyed on the item's Appendix A key rather than on the answer: Appendix A names U+0032 under cl-19, cl-24, cl-25 and cl-27 and under none of those five, so an unstated frame is a well-formed input here whatever class the occurrence turns out to have. With the frame unstated all four key candidates stand and the axis that would separate them is absent, and the construct settles the answer without it. The three entries below record that the answer does not move under classification.ambiguous_context, the question spec/derived/questions.tsv keys for exactly this situation — cl-30 is not reached by a tie-break among surviving key candidates at all, so neither choice of tie-break can select it or unselect it. This is the assertion no enumerating class can make: for cl-30 an unstated frame blocks nothing, because § A.30 states no condition for a frame to satisfy.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ A.30; § 3.1.2's list, which does not name cl-30 and does not name any class Appendix A gives U+0032)
The tie-break Policy::JLREQ selects, which this occurrence never reaches
The other choice spec/derived/questions.tsv records for that question, which this occurrence never reaches either

forbidden.why: Resolving the unstated frame by a tie-break instead of by the construct. § A.19 lists U+0032 with an empty Remarks cell in both locales, so it is the candidate that survives every frame and the one a lowest-class tie-break selects. The occurrence is not ambiguous at all: the construct decides it, and an implementation that reaches for a tie-break here reaches for one inside every tate-chu-yoko whose frame a caller left unstated.

cases.quote: EN: To set strings as tate-chu-yoko (horizontal-in-vertical setting), first set from left to right using solid setting, then align the whole string to the center of the vertical line (Figure 101). When hiragana (cl-15), katakana (cl-16) or ideographic characters (cl-19) are set before/after tate-chu-yoko, the inter-character spacing is set solid. — JA: 縦中横に配置する文字列は，横方向（左から右方向）にベタ組で配置し，その文字列全体を行の中央に配置する（Figure 101）．なお，縦中横の前後に配置する平仮名（cl-15），片仮名（cl-16）又は漢字等（cl-19）との字間は，ベタ組にする．
cases.rationale: This is the boundary the document draws around cl-30, and it draws it by naming the neighbors by their own classes rather than by excluding anything, because § A.30 excludes nothing. The quoted sentence states what happens 「縦中横の前後に配置する平仮名（cl-15），片仮名（cl-16）又は漢字等（cl-19）」 — when hiragana, katakana or ideographic characters are set before or after a tate-chu-yoko — and it has no meaning unless the character before the run keeps the class its own key gives it. If the neighbors were cl-30 the sentence would be about cl-30 against cl-30 and would have named three classes for nothing, and § 3.2.5's Note would not have needed a Table 1 row for cl-30 'and adjacent other character classes'. 第 gets cl-19 without appearing in any Appendix A table: § A.19 states that its table lists the non-ideographic characters of the class, and U+7B2C is a Unified_Ideograph. The occurrence sits immediately before the declared construct, which is what makes it worth asking — an implementation whose construct bleeds one occurrence outwards answers cl-30 here and loses the only sentence JLReq gives for the spacing at this boundary.

forbidden.why: Extending a construct to the occurrence in front of it. § 3.2.5 names cl-15, cl-16 and cl-19 as the classes of the characters set before and after a tate-chu-yoko and states the spacing there in terms of them, and § 3.2.5's Note sends the complete answer to a Table 1 row for cl-30 'and adjacent other character classes'. An implementation that answers cl-30 here has no adjacent other class left to look up.

cases.quote: EN: When hiragana (cl-15), katakana (cl-16) or ideographic characters (cl-19) are set before/after tate-chu-yoko, the inter-character spacing is set solid. — JA: なお，縦中横の前後に配置する平仮名（cl-15），片仮名（cl-16）又は漢字等（cl-19）との字間は，ベタ組にする．
cases.rationale: The mirror of the case above, and not a duplicate of it: the quoted sentence says 前後, before *and* after, and the two sides fail differently. A range in this format is half-open — constructs.tate_chu_yoko[0].items is [1, 3], so item 3 is outside the construct — and an implementation that reads a construct's range as inclusive, or that closes a run one occurrence late, answers cl-30 here while answering the preceding-ideograph case correctly. 回 is a Unified_Ideograph and reaches cl-19 the same way 第 does, so the two cases differ in nothing but which side of the run they ask about.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.19, § 3.2.5's second sentence read on its 後 half)

forbidden.why: Reading the construct's half-open range as inclusive. The character after a tate-chu-yoko is one of the three classes § 3.2.5 names, and the run it follows ends at the occurrence before it.

cases.quote: EN: Setting Latin letters and/or European numerals in tate-chu-yoko (horizontal-in-vertical setting, see Figure 96). Tate-chu-yoko layout is usually adopted when dealing with a two-digit number in European numerals, or a combination of two or three Latin letters, the length of which is equal to the default size of the line in paragraph direction or longer than that just to an acceptable extent. — JA: 縦中横（正常な向きのまま，横組にする）にして配置する（Figure 96）．2桁のアラビア数字，行の幅とほぼ同じ程度かやや行の幅よりはみ出す程度の記号として用いる2文字程度の欧字の文字列では，一般に縦中横にする．
cases.rationale: The second of the two applications the quoted sentence names, and the one that shows the class is not about numerals. § A.30 admits every character, so the two applications § 3.2.3 lists are the usual ones and not the permitted ones: an implementation that recognized tate-chu-yoko only for digits would be reading a sentence about typographic practice as a membership condition. The letters declare the proportional frame because the same paragraph states it — 'Proportional glyphs (or half-width glyphs for European numerals) are used for characters in tate-chu-yoko layout' — and the advances are the caller's own, as ADR 0002 requires. The following hiragana is running text and is here so that the run has the neighbor § 3.2.5 states an answer for.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ A.30, § 3.9.2's entry for cl-30, § 3.2.3's third style)

forbidden.why: The key's answer, reached by not asking which construct the occurrence is in. § A.27 lists U+0054 with the Remark 'proportionally-spaced' (プロポーショナル) and § 3.2.6's Note treats proportional Western characters as cl-27. It is the right answer for the same two letters set the other way § 3.2.3 permits, which is the next case, and the two inputs differ in exactly one thing.

cases.quote: EN: (A combination of two or three Latin letters may be rotated 90 degrees clockwise rather than set in tate-chu-yoko layout.) — JA: （後者の2文字程度の欧字の文字列は，文字を時計回りに90度回転し，配置する方法もある）
cases.rationale: This is the case that says what is nearly a member and is not, and the document says it in so many words. Two Latin letters in a vertical line are exactly the occurrence § 3.2.3 offers two ways of setting, and the parenthetical quoted above is the other way: rotate them ninety degrees clockwise instead. Which way a caller set them is a property of the document rather than of the characters, and it is not a policy question — spec/derived/questions.tsv keys none for it — because it is a choice between two constructs and not between two readings of one rule. So this input differs from the case above in exactly one thing, the `constructs` object, and answers differently. cl-27 is what the key leaves standing: § A.27 lists U+0054 as proportionally-spaced, § A.19 lists it as the folded key of the full-width Ｔ and the proportional frame rules that reading out, and nothing here declares the occurrence a unit symbol, which is the only way § A.25's listing of the same key is reached.

forbidden.why: The misreading § A.30 invites, and the one this file exists to publish. 'Any character may participate in tate-chu-yoko composition' admits every character and excludes none, so an implementation that turns it into a lookup makes every occurrence in every document a member of cl-30 and the other twenty-nine classes unreachable. The sentence is a permission for a construct, not a predicate over characters. Note that spec/derived/classes.tsv records cl-30 with an empty `enumeration` column and spec/derived/appendix-a.tsv holds no cl-30 row at all: both record the absence of a table, and neither records the admission the sentence states.

cases.quote: EN: To typeset a (small) group of characters horizontally within a vertical line of main text. — JA: 縦組の行中で，文字を縦向きのまま横組にすること．
cases.rationale: The same two letters and the same declared frames in horizontal composition, where there is no tate-chu-yoko for an occurrence to be in. The glossary entry quoted above defines the construct as setting characters horizontally *within a vertical line*, and the Japanese half adds 縦向きのまま — the characters keep their upright orientation — which the English half omits and which is what distinguishes tate-chu-yoko from § 3.2.3's rotation style; § 2.3.2 lists it as the third of three ways of setting Latin letters and European numerals in vertical writing mode. So cl-30 is unreachable in horizontal composition. This is a condition on the construct's availability and not on § A.30's sentence, which carries no direction qualifier: spec/derived/rules.tsv marks § 3.2.5 direction_conditional and marks no membership statement, and this case is declared horizontal for that reason rather than to claim that a class is direction-conditional. What JLReq does not state is what an occurrence declared inside a tate-chu-yoko in horizontal composition would be. That is not a permitted alternative and not a silence between two readings but an input the document gives no meaning to, so no case in this file declares one.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.27; the glossary entry for tate-chu-yoko and § 2.3.2 for the construct's availability)

forbidden.why: cl-30 in horizontal composition. The construct the class is named after is defined only 「縦組の行中で」, in a vertical line, and § 2.3.2 introduces it among the differences between the two writing modes. An implementation that answers cl-30 here is answering from the characters, since nothing else in this input could have suggested it.

cases.quote: EN: There is no line break opportunity between two consecutive characters belonging to the same set of characters in tate-chu-yoko (cl-30). If two consecutive characters belong to different sets of characters in tate-chu-yoko (cl-30), there a line break opportunity exists between them. — JA: 後ろに配置する“縦中横中の文字（cl-30）の文字が，前に配置する縦中横中の文字（cl-30）と同一の縦中横のグループに属する場合は，分割不可とする．後ろに配置する縦中横中の文字（cl-30）の文字が，前に配置する縦中横中の文字（cl-30）とは別のグループに属する縦中横の場合は，分割可とする．
cases.rationale: Two tate-chu-yoko groups that abut with no occurrence between them, which is the configuration the quoted note presupposes and the reason cl-30 needs a run identity rather than a class alone: the classes on both sides of the boundary between the runs are identical and the answer at that boundary is the opposite of the answer inside a run. A four-digit year is one way a caller reaches this configuration — the string is too wide for one group, so it is declared as two groups of two digits, which is a caller's choice and not a statement of the document — and the case asserts the class of the first occurrence of the *second* group, the one an implementation that reads only the first entry of the array drops. The classification answer cannot show which group an occurrence is in; that is exactly why the pairing is data in the input rather than an inference (ADR 0008), and why this case asserts membership only. The break answer itself is not stated here: C.2#13 is deferred to M1 in docs/conformance-deferrals.toml, where the boundary case that exercises it is written, so this case names only the rule it exercises. Two properties of the quotation are the published document's and are reproduced rather than repaired: the English is ungrammatical as published ('there a line break opportunity exists between them') and the Japanese carries an unmatched opening quotation mark before 縦中横中の文字. Neither is recorded in spec/derived/defects.tsv. The Japanese is also the authoritative wording, because it says グループ twice while the English says 'the same set of characters in tate-chu-yoko (cl-30)', which read as the class itself makes the note's first sentence contradict its second.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ A.30, § 3.9.2's entry for cl-30; C.2#13 for why the run identity is carried)

forbidden.why: Reading the key for every occurrence a second construct declares. § A.24's Remark 'half-width' and § 3.2.6's Note give cl-24 for a half-width European numeral mixed with Japanese text, and an implementation that answered it here would treat the four digits as one grouped numeral — one object with no interior boundary at all, which is the one thing C.2#13 says this input is not.

cases.quote: EN: In vertical writing mode, characters with superscripts or subscripts, that is ornamented character complex (cl-21) characters, are rotated 90 degrees clock-wise. If the length of the sequence is short enough, the sequence can be set as tate-chu-yoko. — JA: 縦組の中に添え字が付いた文字列（親文字群中の文字（添え字付き）（cl-21））を配置する場合は，文字を時計回りに90度回転し，配置する．文字列が短い場合は縦中横にして配置してもよい．
cases.rationale: The quoted Note puts one occurrence in two construct classes at once — a short ornamented character complex (cl-21) that is set as tate-chu-yoko is inside both constructs, and both § A.21 and § A.30 admit it — which is the situation Appendix A can never produce from a key, and the reason this input declares two construct arrays over one range. What this case asserts is the part the document decides: the ideograph in front of the run keeps its own class whichever of the two the run is read as, because § 3.2.5 states the answer for 「縦中横の前後に配置する……漢字等（cl-19）」 without any condition on what the run contains, and § 3.7.1 says nothing at all about the characters outside the complex. What the document does not decide is the class of the occurrence *inside* both constructs. It states no order between § A.21's membership and § A.30's, and no case in this suite can state one today: docs/design/conformance.md forbids an expectation that is any of several answers, an `adjudicated` case must record each reading with the policy that selects it, and spec/derived/questions.tsv keys no question for this priority — keying it to `classification.ambiguous_context`, which § 3.9.2's silence about a mixed Japanese and Latin context produced, would be inventing a question the document does not ask. The choice is in any case unobservable at every boundary JLReq decides: § 3.7.1 prohibits a break inside a cl-21 sequence and prohibits opening its interior for line adjustment, and C.2#13 and E.2#12 state those same two answers for the interior of one tate-chu-yoko group. The one place it would be observable is the Table 1 row the run's neighbors read, published only as tables/table_en2.pdf and tables/table_ja2.pdf, which spec/PROVENANCE.toml records and which are absent from this tree by design. One further thing this input publishes: cases.schema.json lets two construct arrays name one item, while `Runs::of` in docs/design/api-spine.md returns a single `Construct` for an item, so the occurrence the document places in two constructs has no representation in kumihan today.

permitted.source: JLReq normative (§ 3.9.2, § A.19, § 3.2.5's second sentence, which states its answer for whatever the run contains)

forbidden.why: Letting the tate-chu-yoko swallow the occurrence in front of it. Both construct arrays here name items 2 and 3 and neither names item 1, and § 3.2.5 states the spacing at this boundary in terms of the neighbor's own class.

The same failure through the other construct. § 3.9.2 gives the base characters of an ornamented character complex a class of their own precisely so that the characters *in* the complex are cl-21, and 積 is outside the declared range of both constructs; an implementation whose ranges are off by one fails this case twice for two different reasons and passes it for none.
